executive_assessment.text: Shiselweni/Lubombo vulnerability and named Lubombo survey communities add spatial and social detail, with dated national and survey baselines kept distinct.

Irrigation and reported coping practices show capacity alongside finance, information and tenure barriers. The 2026 harvest estimate and 2026/27 food-security forecast have different evidential status.

geographic_notes.text: Source dated 2021 reports: The 2021 risk profile classifies 60% of residents as medium/high climate-vulnerability; poverty underlies risk, with hotspots in Shiselweni and Lubombo and moderate vulnerability in Hhohho and Manzini.

Source dated 2021 reports: Citing Chuang et al. (2017), the communication reports increasing malaria attributed to climate-associated flooding, especially in Lubombo and Hhohho and in populated lowlands of Manzini and Shiselweni.

Source dated 2021 reports: In 2021, the Climate-Smart Market-Oriented Agriculture Project supported irrigation at Mavulandlela/Ntfonjeni (Hhohho) and Intamakuphila/Ngwempisi (Manzini), emphasizing jobs for women and youth.
The 2021 communication reports over 10,000 irrigated hectares and a further 5,000-hectare Lower Usuthu phase then under development.

Source dated 2024-09-10 reports: FAO agricultural-stress data plotted by IMF show agricultural land in all four provinces under recurring stress from 2020 onward; the figure shows monthly provincial maxima.
Source dated 2026-08-18 reports: The 2025 survey covered Lunkhuntfu and Phafeni (Nkilongo), Mabantaneni and Ntuthwakazi (Lubulini), and Mamisa and Luhlanyeni (Sithobela) in semi-arid Lubombo.

Source dated 2026-08-18 reports: Among surveyed Lubombo households, 96.2% said climate change harmed food production and water access, 96.1% reported harder food availability, and 83.8% worsening water scarcity.
Source dated 2026-08-18 reports: The surveyed Lubombo smallholders were 59.8% women; 62.6% reported unemployment and 66.8% depended primarily on agriculture for livelihoods.

Source dated 2026-08-18 reports: Households most often reported crop diversification (80.1%), changed planting dates (73.9%) and drought-tolerant crops (68.6%); small-scale irrigation was adopted by 19.5%.
Source dated 2026-08-18 reports: Respondents cited finance (83.0%), credit (73.9%), information (68.4%), extension services (54.4%) and insecure land tenure (44.1%) as adaptation barriers.

known_gaps.text: Automated machine-screening is not independent source verification. Routine/default app-use approval does not certify claims or sources. 19 of 20 evidence records and 0 of 0 pathways lack claim-level verification in this remediation; review the linked records before relying on them.
The opened drought profile is a brief overview rather than an independent impact evaluation; no recent subnational drought-outcome study was opened.
Draft collection pending human source review and approval. IDA eligibility is not an FCV classification.
National and selected local examples do not establish district-level coverage or causal attribution.
The bank contains no completed mediated climate-FCV pathway; this is an evidence gap, not evidence of absence.
No inspected source establishes an explicit climate-to-conflict pathway or violence/insecurity disrupting climate adaptation; searched UN Common Country Analysis documents were not fully accessible.
Government vulnerability and programme information is largely based on a 2021 risk assessment; contemporary localized risk, implementation status and independently measured outcomes remain limited.
The 2026 FAO outlook is national and does not disaggregate the projected food-insecurity burden by region or livelihood group.
The Lubombo study is cross-sectional and site-selected; its abstract reports 859 respondents while its methods and sample-allocation table describe 880 as the planned sample.
The IMF provincial stress chart and national impact summaries do not provide subnational household loss estimates or causal attribution to individual climate trends.
Main directly checked the original government communication, IMF report, journal table of adaptation barriers, and FAO harvest/forecast distinctions. No climate-to-violence pathway is inferred.
Lubombo field data are 2025 self-reports from selected communities. Institutional/finance constraints must not be represented as insecurity blocking a named climate project.
Routine/default app-use approval granted by Lindsey Jones on 2026-10-27; independent source verification remains incomplete. Lending eligibility is not an FCV classification.
